anecdotes.title: The dragon-pond horses and King Golden Flower
anecdotes.summary: Dragons of a pond near a deva temple mated with mares to sire fierce dragon-colts, so the land breeds fine horses. A King Golden Flower yoked a dragon to draw his carriage; nearing death he touched its ear with his whip and it submerged forever. Dragon-blooded descendants grew so unruly that the king colluded with the Turks to massacre the whole city, now deserted.

anecdotes.title: The Buddha's footprint of Eastern Cakuri

anecdotes.title: The regent brother and the golden casket
anecdotes.summary: Behind Ascarya Monastery's founding: a king's younger brother, made regent, secretly emasculated himself and sealed the proof in a golden casket against future slander. When falsely accused of adultery he produced the casket and was vindicated; later, redeeming five hundred bulls from castration, his body was restored through compassion. The grateful king built the monastery.

anecdotes.title: Vaiśravaṇa slays the raiding Khan
anecdotes.summary: New Monastery, rich in jewelled images, was repeatedly coveted by kings. When Si Shehu Khan camped nearby to seize its treasure, the guardian deity Vaiśravaṇa appeared in his dream and thrust a spear through his chest; the Khan woke in agony and died before he could confess to the monks.

anecdotes.title: Relics of New Monastery

anecdotes.title: Trapuṣa and Bhallika, the first lay disciples

The two merchants met the newly enlightened Buddha and offered him parched grain and honey, becoming the first to receive the five precepts and ten good deeds; he gave them his hair and nail-parings and, folding his robes and inverting his bowl beneath his staff, showed them the very pattern of the stupa they then built.

anecdotes.title: The colossal Buddhas of Bāmīyāna
anecdotes.summary: At a corner of the mountains by the royal city stands a rock-cut standing Buddha some 140–150 feet high, of golden colour and adorned with gems; nearby a welded copper standing Buddha over a hundred feet tall; and in a monastery east of the city a recumbent Buddha over a thousand feet long, in the posture of entering nirvana.

anecdotes.title: Śāṇakavāsa's everlasting robe
anecdotes.summary: At the Small Marshland a monastery keeps tooth-relics of the Buddha, of a pratyekabuddha and of a gold-wheel king, the iron almsbowl of the arhat Śāṇakavāsa, and his nine-striped hempen saṃghāti robe. Disciple of Ānanda, Śāṇakavāsa vowed his robe would endure until the Dharma's end; it is now slightly diminished, proof of the legend's truth.

activity: A powerful kingdom whose Triple-Gem-revering king casts an eighteen-foot silver Buddha yearly and holds a quinquennial almsgiving. Most of its six thousand monks study the Mahāyāna, though a large monastery east of the city houses some three hundred Śrāvakayāna monks. Xuanzang records many monasteries, relic-stupas and legends here before crossing the Black Range into North India.

anecdotes.title: The Chinese hostage prince's monastery
anecdotes.summary: A monastery east of the city was built for a Chinese hostage prince whom King Kaniṣka of Gandhāra lodged in Kāpiśī in summer, in India in winter and in Gandhāra in spring and autumn. Its walls bear his portrait in Chinese dress; he endowed it for life, and a buried treasure he left for its repair is guarded by a parrot-deity that raised an earthquake when an avaricious king tried to dig it up.

anecdotes.title: Rāhula's self-opening stupa
anecdotes.summary: The minister Rāhula, told in a dream that his new stupa lacked a relic, begged the king for the first offering brought to court next day; intercepting a man bearing a buddha-relic, he climbed the stupa, which opened of itself to receive the relic and closed on the hem of his robe. Black aromatic oil has oozed from the crevice ever since, and music is sometimes heard there at night.

anecdotes.title: The novice reborn as a vengeful nāga
anecdotes.summary: A resentful novice, envying the nāga king who fed his arhat master, vowed by his merit to kill the nāga and usurp him; reborn as a nāga he did so and raised storms to destroy the lakeside monastery. King Kaniṣka rebuilt it seven times; after a contest of power and a flame from the king's shoulders the nāga submitted, on condition a watchman strike a sounding instrument whenever a black cloud arose.

anecdotes.title: Relics of the Old Royal and Old Queen's monasteries
anecdotes.summary: Old Royal Monastery keeps a deciduous tooth of Śākyamuni as a bodhisattva, a piece of the Tathāgata's skull-bone with visible hair-pores, and a curled dark-purple hair of his head; the Old Queen's Monastery has a hundred-foot gilt-copper stupa over a measure of the Buddha's relic bones that emits a monthly ring of light.

anecdotes.title: Dīpaṃkara's prophecy and the muddy ground
anecdotes.summary: At a 300-foot Aśoka stupa east of the city, in a former life the future Śākyamuni (then a young ascetic) spread a deerskin and his own hair over muddy ground for Dīpaṃkara Buddha to tread on, and received from him the prediction of his own buddhahood. Flowers descend on the spot on fast days.

anecdotes.title: The Buddha's Shadow Cave and the nāga Gopāla
anecdotes.summary: A cowherd, reprimanded by the king, vowed in hatred to be reborn a destroying nāga and leapt to his death, becoming the nāga Gopāla of a deep gully cave. The Buddha flew from Central India, calmed his malice, and on the nāga's plea left his shadow-image in the cave, with five arhats to receive the nāga's offerings until the Dharma's end.

anecdotes.title: The relics of Hilo city
anecdotes.summary: In a storied pavilion at Hilo are kept the Buddha's skull-bone (twelve inches round, with visible hair-pores), his lotus-leaf-shaped cranial bone, an eyeball as large as a crabapple, his yellow-red robe and his ringed pewter staff. Pilgrims take fragrant impressions of the skull-bone to read their fortunes; the attendants charge a gold coin to view it, yet worshippers only multiply.

activity: The heartland of Gandhāran Buddhism, its capital Puruṣapura now under Kāpiśī and its thousand monasteries fallen to ruin. Xuanzang records it as the birthplace of the great commentators — Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, Dharmatrāta, Manoratha, Pārśva and others — and venerates King Kaniṣka's colossal stupa, the site of the Buddha's almsbowl, and the Vessantara (Sudāna) jātaka sites; monks of both the Śrāvakayāna and the Mahāyāna are noted at its outlying monasteries.

anecdotes.title: King Kaniṣka's great stupa and the cowherd's prophecy
anecdotes.summary: The Buddha foretold to Ānanda that four hundred years after his demise a King Kaniṣka would raise a stupa here over most of his relics. Chasing a vanishing white hare, Kaniṣka found a cowherd building a small three-foot stupa as the prophesied sign; converted, he encased it in a stone stupa over four hundred feet high, but the small stupa kept rising three feet higher until he yielded. He enshrined a measure of the Buddha's relic bones beneath gilded copper disks.

anecdotes.title: The Buddha's almsbowl, now in Persia
anecdotes.summary: Within the royal city stood the precious terrace where the Buddha's almsbowl was once kept; venerated here for several hundred years after his demise, it was later carried through various countries and is now in Persia.

anecdotes.title: Venerable Pārśva who would not lie down
anecdotes.summary: Ordained a monk only at eighty and mocked as a useless old man, Pārśva vowed never to lie down with his ribs touching the mat until he had mastered the Tripiṭaka, severed the desires of the three realms and gained the six powers and eight emancipations. In three years he achieved it, and was honoured as 'Venerable Ribs'.

anecdotes.title: Manoratha's death and Vasubandhu's vindication
anecdotes.summary: In King Vikramāditya's rigged debate the śāstra master Manoratha defeated ninety-nine heretics but was shouted down on the last point and, shamed, bit off his tongue and died, writing to his disciple Vasubandhu of the futility of arguing among partisans. When a new king reigned, Vasubandhu summoned the same heretics, reiterated his teacher's arguments, and routed them, clearing Manoratha's name.

Once 1,400 monasteries and 18,000 monks lined the Śubhavastu River, now much decayed. Xuanzang records a dense cluster of jātaka stupas around the capital Maṅgala.

anecdotes.title: The ṛṣi Patience mutilated by King Kali
anecdotes.summary: A stupa east of Maṅgala marks where the Buddha, in a former life as the ascetic Kṣāntivādin ('Patience'), had his limbs cut off one by one by King Kali yet felt no anger.

anecdotes.title: The taming of the Apalāla dragon
anecdotes.summary: At the source of the Śubhavastu River, a wronged exorcist reborn as the malignant Apalāla dragon blighted the crops with white water. The Buddha sent Vajrapāṇi, who struck the cliffs with his thunderbolt and terrified the dragon into taking refuge; the Buddha forbade it to ruin the harvests but allowed it to flood once every twelve years.

anecdotes.title: The dragon-girl and the founding of Udyāna's kings
anecdotes.summary: A fugitive Śākya, carried by a wild goose to a mountain lake, transformed a dragon-king's daughter into human form by the power of his merit and married her. Armed with the dragon-king's hidden sword he slew the king of Udyāna and seized the throne; his son became King Uttarasena, who later obtained a share of the Buddha's relics for his stupa.

anecdotes.title: Prince Kuṇāla's torn-out eyes
anecdotes.summary: Aśoka's son Kuṇāla, governor of Takṣaśilā, was destroyed by a forged order sealed with the king's tooth-marks by his vengeful stepmother; obeying it, he had his eyes torn out and wandered as a blind beggar. Recognised by his singing in the royal stable, he was restored to sight when the arhat Ghoṣa washed his eyes with the tears wept by a whole assembly hearing the Dharma.

anecdotes.title: Prince Mahāsattva and the starving tigress
anecdotes.summary: At a great rocky pass Prince Mahāsattva, pitying a starving tigress too weak to eat, pricked himself with bamboo to give her his blood and let her devour him. The soil and plants there are still dark red as if blood-stained, and visitors feel an involuntary dread.

activity: A mountain-ringed kingdom, the great seat of Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma learning, where Xuanzang stayed about two years studying. Over a hundred monasteries hold more than five thousand monks, with four relic-stupas of Aśoka. He recounts the founding of the land by the arhat Madhyāntika, King Kaniṣka's great council that compiled the Vibhāṣā, and the cells of later śāstra masters Saṃghabhadra, Skandhila, Pūrṇa and Bodhila.

anecdotes.title: Madhyāntika drains the dragon-lake
anecdotes.summary: Fulfilling the Buddha's prophecy to Ānanda, the arhat Madhyāntika came fifty years after the nirvana, asked the lake's dragon-king for only enough room for his knees, then magically expanded until the dragon yielded the whole drained lake; on it he founded five hundred monasteries, and Kaśmīra became a Buddhist land.

anecdotes.title: King Kaniṣka's council and the Vibhāṣā
anecdotes.summary: Puzzled by the discord of the schools, King Kaniṣka and Venerable Pārśva gathered 499 masters in Kaśmīra and, with Vasumitra (who proved his stature by tossing a thread the devas caught) as president, compiled vast commentaries on the Sūtra, Vinaya and Abhidharma — three hundred thousand stanzas. Kaniṣka had them incised on copper plates, sealed in a stupa, and guarded by yakṣas.

anecdotes.title: The Buddha's tooth carried by elephants
anecdotes.summary: A monk returning from India was carried off by a herd of elephants to heal a sick elephant's foot; in gratitude they gave him a golden casket holding a Buddha's tooth-relic. After a river-dragon forced him to surrender it, he studied dragon-subduing for three years, returned, and recovered the tooth, enshrining it in a monastery whose stupa emits light on fast days.

anecdotes.title: The descent from Trāyastriṃśa Heaven

anecdotes.summary: The Ṛṣi of the Big Tree, his passion roused by King Brahmadatta's daughters, demanded one in marriage; only the youngest consented. Enraged at being given the plainest, the ṛṣi cursed the other ninety-nine to become hunchbacked and remain unmarried for life — and so the old capital Kusumapura became known as the City of Hunchbacked Maidens.

anecdotes.title: The accession of Harṣavardhana
anecdotes.summary: When King Śaśāṅka of Karṇasuvarṇa lured and murdered King Rājyavardhana, the leaderless country fell into chaos. The minister Bhaṇḍi and the court pressed Rājyavardhana's younger brother Harṣavardhana to take the throne; after consulting the oracle of an Avalokiteśvara image on the Ganges, he accepted, to avenge his brother and restore the kingdom.

Its several hundred monasteries are mostly ruined, the few monks following the Saṃmitīya school of the Śrāvakayāna. anecdotes.title: Anāthapiṇḍika and the gift of Jetavana
anecdotes.summary: Elder Sudatta — called Anāthapiṇḍika, 'Giver of Alms to the Poor and Helpless', for his charity — adored the Buddha and built him a temple in Prince Jeta's garden south of Śrāvastī, the famous Jetavana, marked now by two seventy-foot Aśoka pillars topped with a wheel and a bull.

anecdotes.title: The conversion of Aṅgulimāla
anecdotes.summary: Aṅgulimāla, a murderer who strung his victims' finger-bones into a garland and was about to kill his own mother to complete it, rushed at the Buddha to slay him too; though he ran, he could not overtake the slowly-walking World-honoured One. Struck by the Buddha's words, he renounced his evil, took refuge, and attained arhatship.

activity: The heartland of Buddhist India and the central stage of Xuanzang's journey. The land is fertile, growing the fragrant 'rice for great personages'; the people esteem learning and revere the Dharma, with over fifty monasteries and more than ten thousand monks (mostly Mahāyāna) alongside many deva temples. South of the Ganges lies the ancient city of Kusumapura, later Pāṭaliputra, the old capital to which Aśoka moved from Rājagṛha. Xuanzang surveys Aśoka's surviving relics — the stone pillar at his former 'hell', a stupa holding the Buddha's relic bones, the footprint-stone, and Kukkuṭārāma Monastery.

anecdotes.title: King Aśoka's hell
anecdotes.summary: Early in his cruel reign Aśoka built a torture-prison whose jailer killed all who entered. A young śramaṇa, condemned there, gained arhatship when thrown into a cauldron that turned to a cool lotus pond. Recognising the rule that all who enter must die, the king had the jailer cast into the furnace, then abolished the hell and showed leniency.

anecdotes.title: Aśoka and the eighty-four thousand stupas
anecdotes.summary: Converted by the arhat Upagupta, Aśoka commanded the spirits to build stupas for the Buddha's relics throughout Jambudvīpa; the arhat eclipsed the sun with his hand as the signal to enshrine them all at one instant.

anecdotes.title: Nāgārjuna, Deva and the silenced bell
anecdotes.summary: After heretics defeated the monks of Pāṭaliputra and forbade them to strike the assembly bell for twelve years, Nāgārjuna's disciple Deva entered the city in disguise, struck the bell, and in twelve days vanquished all the heretics in debate; a stupa commemorates his victory.

anecdotes.title: Aśvaghoṣa and the demon-eloquent brahman
anecdotes.summary: A brahman who debated only from behind a curtain owed his eloquence to a served demon. Aśvaghoṣa exposed him by lifting the curtain mid-debate; the brahman lost his fame in a single morning.

anecdotes.title: Aśoka's last gift of half a myrobalan
anecdotes.summary: Dying and stripped of power by his ministers, Aśoka found he commanded only half an āmalaka fruit from his meal; he sent it to Kukkuṭārāma Monastery as his final alms, and the monks enshrined its kernel in a stupa.

activity: South-west of Pāṭaliputra, the first of a chain of great monasteries Xuanzang passed on the road to Gayā. Built by the last descendant of King Bimbisāra, Tilaḍhāka has four courts, lofty three-storied pavilions and three shrines housing a thirty-foot standing Buddha flanked by Tārā and Avalokiteśvara cast in brass, each shrine holding the Buddha's relic bones. Its thousands of monks all study the Mahāyāna. Further along this road stand Guṇamati Monastery and Śīlabhadra Monastery, named for two śāstra masters who humbled famous opponents.

anecdotes.title: Guṇamati subdues the Sāṃkhya master Mādhava
anecdotes.summary: Guṇamati of South India challenged the celebrated Sāṃkhya brahman Mādhava; after days of debate Mādhava died vomiting blood, and his widow fled when Guṇamati told her 'the one who can subjugate you has been subjugated by me.' The monastery on the spur of the hill marks the victory.

anecdotes.title: Śīlabhadra defeats the South-Indian heretic
anecdotes.summary: As a young disciple of Dharmapāla at Nālandā, the thirty-year-old Śīlabhadra — a prince of Samataṭa — refuted a renowned South-Indian heretic; rewarded with the revenue of a city, he built the monastery that bears his name. He would later become Xuanzang's own teacher at Nālandā.

East lies Prāgbodhi ('Pre-enlightenment') Mountain, which the Bodhisattva climbed before his awakening; warned by the mountain-god that it could not bear his enlightenment, he left his shadow in a dragon's cave and went on toward the bodhi tree.

anecdotes.title: The Bodhisattva on Prāgbodhi Mountain
anecdotes.summary: Having abandoned six years' austerities and taken milk-gruel, the Bodhisattva climbed Prāgbodhi seeking enlightenment, but the earth quaked and the mountain-god declared it no fit place. Beings of the Heaven of Pure Abode directed him south-west to the pipal tree and its diamond seat; he left his shadow in a blind dragon's cave to console it and departed.

activity: The supreme holy site of the journey: the place of the Buddha's enlightenment. The enclosure is girt by high, strong brick walls about five hundred paces in circuit, long from east to west and narrow from north to south, with four gates — the main (east) gate opening toward the Nairañjanā River, the south gate beside a large flower-pond, the west side an inaccessible natural barrier, and the north gate leading to Mahābodhi Monastery. At the centre is the diamond seat (vajrāsana / bodhimaṇḍa), said to have arisen with the great earth at the start of the present kalpa, made of diamond and over a hundred paces in circuit, where every buddha of the age attains awakening; it alone stays stable when the earth quakes. Two east-facing statues of Avalokiteśvara stand at the south and north limits of the enclosure, their gradual sinking foretelling the Dharma's decline (the south one has already sunk to the chest). Over the pipal bodhi tree itself — repeatedly cut down (by Aśoka before his conversion, by his heretical queen, and lately by King Śaśāṅka) and each time revived, last walled to twenty-four feet by King Pūrṇavarman. East of the tree rises the great Mahābodhi shrine, some 160–170 feet high on a base over twenty paces wide, of brick plastered with lime, its tiered niches full of golden images, crowned with a gilded copper āmalaka finial, the inner chamber flanked at its outer door by silver images of Avalokiteśvara and Maitreya over ten feet tall, and holding the famous earth-touching image said to have been finished by Maitreya himself. The whole enclosure is packed with stupas and shrines raised by the kings, ministers and nobles of every land of Jambudvīpa, set 'as closely together as the scales of a fish'; outside the north gate stands Mahābodhi Monastery, built by a king of Siṃhala for its pilgrim-monks, where fewer than a thousand monks study both the Mahāyāna and the Sthavira schools.

anecdotes.title: Śaśāṅka's assault on the bodhi tree and image
anecdotes.summary: King Śaśāṅka, a Śaivite, felled the bodhi tree, burned its roots and soaked them with sugarcane juice, yet King Pūrṇavarman revived it with the milk of a thousand cows and walled it to twenty-four feet. Śaśāṅka also ordered the great image replaced by one of Maheśvara, but the minister instead walled it up and lit a lamp; the king soon died of blistering sores.

anecdotes.title: Maitreya finishes the earth-touching image
anecdotes.summary: A brahman sealed himself in the shrine to make the Buddha's image, asking that the door stay shut six months; opened four days early, the chamber was empty but for the finished earth-touching (bhūmisparśa) image, all but a spot above the breast. A monk dreamed the maker was Maitreya Bodhisattva, who had made the right hand point downward to recall the earth's witness against Māra.

anecdotes.title: Indra the grass-cutter and the diamond seat
anecdotes.summary: Before his awakening the Bodhisattva sought clean grass for a seat; Indra, disguised as a grass-cutter, offered him a bundle which he spread on the diamond seat. A stupa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka, stands south of the bodhi tree at the spot where the grass was received.

anecdotes.title: Māra's assault and the lotus weapons
anecdotes.summary: The King of Māras arrayed his demon host with storm, thunder, fire and weapons to drive the Bodhisattva from the seat, but in his meditation of great compassion every spear and arrow turned into lotus flowers and the host fled in disorder; his daughters who came to seduce the Bodhisattva were changed into decrepit old women. Two stupas east of the tree mark the place.

anecdotes.title: Mucilinda the dragon king shelters the Buddha
anecdotes.summary: In a wood east of Indra's pool lies the clear pond of the dragon king Mucilinda; after his enlightenment the Buddha meditated there seven days while the dragon coiled his body seven times about him and spread his many heads above as a canopy.

anecdotes.title: The two milkmaids' gruel
anecdotes.summary: At the south-west corner outside the enclosure three stupas mark the house of the two milkmaids who offered milk-gruel, the spot where they cooked it, and where the Tathāgata received it — ending the six years of austerities before his enlightenment.

anecdotes.title: The Mahābodhi Monastery of the Siṃhala king
anecdotes.summary: After a Siṃhala monk was scorned in Indian monasteries, the king of Siṃhala obtained leave from the king of India to build a monastery at the holiest site; its monks, mostly from the Land of Lions, observe the Vinaya strictly and study both vehicles.

activity: East of the bodhi tree, beyond the Mahā River and a great jungle, Xuanzang reached Kukkuṭapāda ('Cock's Foot', also Gurupāda, 'Sage's Foot') Mountain, where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa entered nirvana. Holding the Buddha's golden-thread kaṣāya, Kāśyapa caused the three peaks to close over him, there to await Maitreya and hand on the robe. North-east lie Buddhavana Mountain, with its fragrant sandalwood rock and the latent five hundred arhats, and Yaṣṭi ('Stick') Wood, where the layman Jayasena made seven koṭis of clay 'Dharma-relic' stupas over thirty years.

anecdotes.title: Mahākāśyapa awaits Maitreya within the peaks
anecdotes.summary: Twenty years after the Buddha's nirvana, Kāśyapa climbed the mountain bearing the Buddha's golden kaṣāya for Maitreya; by the power of his vow the three peaks closed about him. When Maitreya comes he will snap his fingers, the peaks will open, and Kāśyapa will hand over the robe before cremating himself in self-kindled fire.

anecdotes.title: The brahman who could not measure the Buddha
anecdotes.summary: In Yaṣṭi Wood a doubting brahman used a sixteen-foot bamboo to measure the Buddha's height, but the figure always exceeded it by sixteen feet; he cast the pole down and it took root as the bamboo grove.

activity: The old capital of Magadha, ringed by hills. Within the former Kuśāgrapura and the later city of Rājagṛha ('Royal House') cluster the central scenes of the Buddha's ministry: Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak), where over his fifty-year career he often preached and delivered the Lotus Sutra; the Kalandaka Bamboo Garden, his frequent residence; the hot springs of Vipula Hill; and Pippala Cave. South-west of the Bamboo Garden is the cave where Mahākāśyapa and 999 arhats compiled the Tripiṭaka after the nirvana — the First Council — beside the hall built for them by King Ajātaśatru, with the 'Great Congregation' collection gathered separately nearby.

anecdotes.title: The First Council at the cave of Mahākāśyapa
anecdotes.summary: After the Buddha's nirvana Mahākāśyapa summoned the saints by striking a bell on Mount Sumeru; 999 arhats assembled in a cave south-west of the Bamboo Garden. Ānanda, at first excluded as still 'in training', attained arhatship overnight and entered through the keyhole; Ānanda recited the Sutras, Upāli the Vinaya, and Kāśyapa the Abhidharma — the Assembly of the Elder.

anecdotes.title: Devadatta and the intoxicated elephant
anecdotes.summary: At the north gate Devadatta, plotting with Ajātaśatru, loosed the drunken elephant Dhanapāla at the Buddha, who produced five lions from his fingertips and tamed it.

anecdotes.title: Śāriputra's awakening through Aśvajit
anecdotes.summary: Near the city the layman Śāriputra met the arhat Aśvajit on almsround; struck by his serene bearing he asked his teacher's doctrine, and on hearing a single verse of the Dharma attained the first stage of sainthood.

anecdotes.title: Bimbisāra's road and the relic stupas
anecdotes.summary: King Bimbisāra built stepped roads up Vulture Peak to hear the Dharma; east of the Bamboo Garden King Ajātaśatru raised a stupa over his share of the Buddha's relics, beside another holding half of Ānanda's body, divided between Magadha and Vaiśālī.

monasteries.text: a single walled complex of monasteries built by six successive kings

activity: The greatest monastic university of India and the goal of Xuanzang's pilgrimage, where he studied for about five years under the centenarian śāstra master Śīlabhadra. It lies more than thirty li north of Rājagṛha on land that was once a mango grove, bought by five hundred merchants with ten koṭis of gold and given to the Buddha, who preached there three months. The complex grew by the patronage of six successive kings, each adding a monastery: Śakrāditya raised the first (its Buddha-image hall where forty monks dine daily in the founders' honour); his son Buddhagupta built to the south; Tathāgatagupta to the east; Bālāditya to the north-east, with a great temple over three hundred feet high resembling the great shrine at the bodhi tree; Bālāditya's son Vajra to the west; and a king of Central India to the north — the whole then enclosed by one lofty wall with a single gate. Among the surrounding monuments are a temple over two hundred feet high where the Buddha preached four months, the unfinished Brass Temple of King Śīlāditya (Harṣa) planned to reach a hundred feet, an eighty-foot copper standing Buddha made by King Pūrṇavarman beneath a six-storey pavilion, a brick temple of Tārā Bodhisattva drawing New-Year crowds, a stupa holding the Buddha's hair and nail relics, the willow-twig tree, and a great well inside the south gate. Its several thousand monks are brilliant scholars who admit visitors only after a gatekeeper's examination — seven or eight of ten challengers flee defeated. Xuanzang names its luminaries: Dharmapāla, Candragupta, Guṇamati, Sthiramati, Prabhāmitra, Viśeṣamitra, Jñānacandra and Śīlabhadra.

anecdotes.title: The dragon Nālandā and the founding prophecy
anecdotes.summary: The monastery took its name from a dragon dwelling in a mango-grove pond, or from a former bodhisattva-king 'Insatiable in Almsgiving'. When Śakrāditya began building, the dragon's body was pierced; a Jain diviner foretold the monastery would flourish over a thousand years and become the standard of all India, though students would often spit blood because the dragon had been hurt.

anecdotes.title: The two saintly monks from China
anecdotes.summary: At Bālāditya's inaugural feast two latecomer monks said they had come from China; recognised as saints, they vanished before the king could greet them. His deepened faith led him to renounce the throne and become a monk — and, ranked lowest among the monks, he had the rule made that the unordained take seniority by age.

anecdotes.title: The relic stupa of the Buddha's hair and nails
anecdotes.summary: South of a standing Avalokiteśvara statue near the monastery is a stupa keeping hair and fingernail relics that the Buddha shaved and clipped over a three-month period; sick people are often cured of their illnesses by circumambulating it.

anecdotes.title: The willow-twig tree
anecdotes.summary: Within the enclosure stands a tree grown from a willow twig the Tathāgata used to clean his teeth and threw to the ground; though ages have passed its two branches never increase nor decrease in number.

anecdotes.title: The great well inside the south gate
anecdotes.summary: When thirsting merchants came to the Buddha, he pointed at the earth and the merchant-lord dug with a cart-axle until water gushed forth; all who drank and heard the Dharma became enlightened. The great well inside the south gate marks the spot.

activity: The chain of sites east and south of Nālandā by which Xuanzang left Magadha for Īraṇaparvata. He passed Kolika, birthplace of Maudgalaputra, and Kālapināka, birthplace of Śāriputra; Indraśailaguhā ('Indra's Cave') Mountain, where Indra inscribed forty-two questions answered by the Buddha; Kapotaka ('Pigeon') Monastery, whose more than two hundred monks study the Sarvāstivāda school; a hilltop image of Avalokiteśvara sought by the Siṃhala king; and a further monastery of some fifty monks following the older 'gradual' (Śrāvakayāna) teaching, before reaching Lāvaṇīla and turning east toward Īraṇaparvata.

anecdotes.title: The Buddha as the self-sacrificing pigeon
anecdotes.summary: At Kapotaka a bird-catcher who caught nothing all day came to the preaching Buddha; the Tathāgata took the form of a pigeon and burned himself in a fire to feed the man's family, who later converted. The monastery is named for the pigeon.

anecdotes.title: The wild goose that died for the monks
anecdotes.summary: At Indraśailaguhā monks who followed the older teaching ate the three kinds of pure meat; when a monk jokingly hailed a passing flock, one goose fell dead before him. Shamed, the monks renounced meat-eating, embraced the Mahāyāna, and built the Haṃsa ('Wild Goose') Stupa over the bird.

anecdotes.title: Birthplaces of Śāriputra and Maudgalaputra
anecdotes.summary: Stupas built by King Aśoka mark Kolika, where Maudgalaputra was born and entered nirvana, and Kālapināka, the birthplace of Śāriputra; the lifelong friends renounced the world together and became the Buddha's foremost disciples in miraculous power and in wisdom.

activity: A vast country (over ten thousand li in circuit) of short, dark, hot-tempered but diligent people who worship gods and do not believe in the buddha-dharma — so no monastery has ever been built and the few believers keep the faith privately, amid several hundred deva temples. activity: A mountain-girt country of Central India (the southern Kosala) whose kṣatriya king deeply honours the Dharma. Over a hundred monasteries hold nearly ten thousand monks, all Mahāyāna, with over seventy deva temples. South of the city an old monastery and an Aśoka stupa mark where the Buddha subdued heretics and where Nāgārjuna later dwelt under the patronage of King Śātavāha; south-west rises Bhrāmaragiri ('Black Bee') Mountain, the five-tiered rock monastery the king carved for Nāgārjuna.

anecdotes.title: Deva's needle in Nāgārjuna's bowl
anecdotes.summary: Deva came from Siṃhala to debate Nāgārjuna, who sent out a bowl brimful of water; Deva silently dropped in a needle. Nāgārjuna, reading the sign — water as his all-embracing wisdom, the needle as Deva fathoming its depths — welcomed him at once, and Deva became his disciple.

anecdotes.title: Nāgārjuna, the gold-making, and his self-sacrifice
anecdotes.summary: Nāgārjuna's elixirs prolonged his and King Śātavāha's lives for centuries and turned the rocks of Bhrāmaragiri to gold to finish the king's mountain monastery. When the king's son, told that his father would die only when the bodhisattva did, begged Nāgārjuna's head, the sage cut his own throat with a blade of dry grass.

activity: Also called Great Andhra: a fertile but thinly-settled country of South India. activity: The 'Land of Lions', an island south of India that Xuanzang appended though he did not personally reach it (compiled from Sinhalese monks). Buddhism was brought by Aśoka's brother Mahendra; several hundred monasteries hold more than twenty thousand monks of both the Mahāyāna and Sthavira schools, split since two centuries after the faith's arrival into the Mahāvihāra sect (which rejected the Mahāyāna and upheld the older tenets) and the Abhayagiri sect (which studied both vehicles). Beside the palace stands the lofty Temple of the Buddha's Tooth, crowned with a ruby that shines like a star, and a great kitchen fed eighteen thousand monks daily. At the south-east corner Laṅkā Mountain is where the Buddha delivered the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra.

anecdotes.title: The lion-ancestor and the naming of Siṃhala
anecdotes.summary: A South-Indian princess carried off by a lion bore a son who slew his lion-father; banished by sea, he reached this gem-island and founded a line named Siṃhala ('lion-taker') after their origin — and the tale is told as a past life of the Buddha.

anecdotes.title: The merchant Siṃhala and the rākṣasīs
anecdotes.summary: The merchant-lord Siṃhala, shipwrecked on the island, was lured with five hundred companions by demon-women (rākṣasīs); warned in a dream, he escaped on the heavenly horse Bālāha, later returned with an army to destroy the iron city, and became the island's king.

anecdotes.title: The Buddha's Tooth and the bowing image
anecdotes.summary: The Temple of the Buddha's Tooth, bathed thrice daily by the king, is crowned with a great ruby; in a nearby shrine a golden Buddha bowed its head to let a thief take the gem from its crown, and so its head remains inclined.

activity: A large, martial country of proud, vengeful people and wine-fed war-elephants, ruled by the astute kṣatriya king Pulakeśin — the one realm the great King Śīlāditya (Harṣa) repeatedly invaded but never subdued. anecdotes.title: Pulakeśin defies Harṣa

activity: A long, narrow old territory of Tukhāra winding along the Oxus between two mountain ranges, breeding hardy small horses; its green-eyed people are rough and irreligious. More than ten monasteries hold few monks; the capital, Khamdādh, has a cliff-cut monastery founded after a king, deceived by a temple-priest over his dying son, turned to a wandering arhat and embraced the Dharma. Its great temple holds a stone Buddha under a copper canopy that turns as worshippers circumambulate it.

anecdotes.title: The king, the lying priest, and the arhat
anecdotes.summary: When the king's son fell ill a deva-temple priest falsely swore he would recover; a wandering arhat foretold the boy's death, which came to pass. The enraged king had the priest killed and the idol cast into the Oxus, then took the arhat as his guide and built the first monastery, and the Dharma flourished.

anecdotes.title: The self-turning canopy
anecdotes.summary: In the great temple a gilded copper canopy over the stone Buddha turns with anyone who circumambulates the image and stops when they stop; Xuanzang examined it and could not determine the cause.

activity: A country of alternating mountains and valleys yielding grapes and orpiment, whose fierce mountain-gods must be appeased by travellers. Its king is of Śākya stock and reveres the Dharma, so the people are all pure Buddhists; there are two monasteries with very few monks. activity: A Pamir country whose capital stands on a rocky ridge backed by the Sītā River, reached over icy passes. Its people have pure faith: over ten monasteries hold more than five hundred monks of the Sarvāstivāda school of the Śrāvakayāna, and the devout king claims descent from 'Chinese sun-god stock' (Cīnadevagotra). His old palace was made into a monastery for the venerable Kumāralāta, founder of the Sautrāntika school and one of the 'Four Brilliant Suns' (with Aśvaghoṣa, Deva and Nāgārjuna).

anecdotes.title: The Chinese princess and the sun-god
anecdotes.summary: A Chinese bride bound for Persia was stranded on a lofty peak during a revolt and found to be pregnant by a man who came daily from the sun's disc; her son, born there, could fly and command the wind, founding the royal line that claims 'Chinese sun-god stock', his mummy still honoured in a mountain cave.

anecdotes.title: Kumāralāta, founder of the Sautrāntika
anecdotes.summary: The king captured the renowned śāstra master Kumāralāta of Takṣaśilā — reciting and writing 32,000 words a day, founder of the Sautrāntika school and counted among the 'Four Brilliant Suns' — and built him a monastery from the old palace.

activity: A walled, well-watered country of two rivers, its writing like Gostana's, reached by crossing the Sītā River and a sandy range. The people piously revere the Triple Gem: several tens of monasteries, most in ruins, hold about a hundred monks who study the Mahāyāna. A southern mountain of cliff-caves and stupas drew Indian arhats by levitation — three still sit there in the samādhi of extinction — and the country holds an unrivalled store of Mahāyāna scriptures, some titles of a hundred thousand stanzas each.

activity: The great jade- and silk-producing oasis of the southern Tarim and the last country of the Record, where Xuanzang lingered before re-entering China. Its cultured, learning-loving people use an India-derived script and love music; over a hundred monasteries hold more than five thousand monks who mostly study the Mahāyāna. The brave king claims descent from the deity Vaiśravaṇa, whose 'earth-nipple' nursed the founding prince — hence the country's name. Its sacred sites include Gośṛṅga ('Cowhorn') Mountain, where the Buddha foretold a Mahāyāna kingdom, the monastery of the arhat Vairocana who first brought the Dharma, and Dīrghabhāvana, holding a Buddha-image that came of itself from Kuci.

anecdotes.title: The earth-nipple and the line of Vaiśravaṇa
anecdotes.summary: A childless king prayed at the shrine of Vaiśravaṇa and a baby burst from the image's forehead; when it refused milk, the earth before the image swelled into a nipple that nursed it — so the prince was reared and the country named 'earth-nipple' (Gostana), its royal line tracing to the deity.

anecdotes.title: The rats that routed the Huns
anecdotes.summary: Golden- and silver-haired desert rats, large as hedgehogs, were revered as divine; when a vast Hun army camped by their mounds, the outnumbered king prayed to them, and that night they gnawed through the enemy's harness and bowstrings, delivering victory.

anecdotes.title: Gośṛṅga (Cowhorn) Mountain and the Buddha's prophecy
anecdotes.summary: At Cowhorn Mountain the Buddha briefly preached and foretold that a Mahāyāna kingdom would arise here; in its cave an arhat sits in the samādhi of extinction awaiting Maitreya, its entrance lately sealed by a rockfall guarded by black wasps.
